levels.name: Beginner
levels.subtitle: Foundations
levels.description: Start from zero. Understand data, use a spreadsheet, read basic SQL and Python, and explain what a number actually means.

levels.name: Intermediate
levels.subtitle: Applied Skills
levels.description: Solve complete analytics tasks: clean data, join tables, explore patterns, design reports, and make your work reproducible.

levels.name: Advanced
levels.subtitle: Specialized Mastery
levels.description: Build robust analytics and engineering workflows, evaluate models and experiments, and operate safely in the cloud.

levels.name: Expert
levels.subtitle: Industry Systems
levels.description: Design governed, monitored, scalable systems for streaming, distributed data and responsible generative AI.

modules.title: Think like a data analyst
modules.outcome: Turn an imprecise business request into a testable metric and an appropriate decision.
modules.prerequisites: None — suitable for someone who has never used analytics software.
modules.lesson: An analyst is not someone who simply makes charts; an analyst converts a decision into a question that can be answered using evidence. First name the audience and the action they may take. Then define precisely what is counted, the time period, and what one record represents. A metric is only meaningful when its numerator and denominator use the same population and date window. Finally distinguish what the dataset directly shows from why you think it happened. This prevents a plausible story from being mistaken for proof.
modules.caseStudy: A delivery team says “service has become worse”. You have daily on-time and total delivery counts for East and West. The manager must decide where to investigate. Instead of plotting every available field, compare weekly on-time delivery rate for both regions and note missing dates.
steps: Write the decision and its owner
Choose the grain and define the metric
Compare equal time windows and count missing records
Explain the observed pattern and propose a check
modules.workedExample: Week 1: 81 on-time / 90 deliveries = 90%; Week 2: 72 on-time / 90 deliveries = 80%. The change is −10 percentage points, not −10 deliveries.
modules.interpretation: The rate declined, but this does not establish why: staffing, weather and route mix may differ. Check these before recommending a policy change.
modules.microProject: On your phone, draft one question about a shop with falling sales, specifying measure, period, comparison and decision.
modules.modelAnswer: “Which shop had the largest week-over-week decline in net revenue over the last four complete weeks, and is it due to order count or average order value?”
modules.commonMistake: Do not treat a correlation or a percentage change as a causal explanation.
modules.next: Take F02 and the Data Analysis course, week 1.

modules.title: Spreadsheet literacy and formulas
modules.outcome: Build a clean table and calculate totals, averages and rates with correct references.
topics: SUM, AVERAGE, IF and basic charts
modules.prerequisites: F01; ability to type or paste values into a grid.
modules.lesson: Each row should represent one observation and each column a single field. Keep a header row, do not merge cells inside the dataset, and store numeric prices as numbers rather than strings with currency symbols. A formula begins with = and changes automatically when input cells change. Relative references move when a formula is copied; a fixed $ reference does not. Structured tables are preferred to scattered ranges because they expand with new data. A chart is a view of a clearly defined calculation, not a substitute for a valid one.
modules.caseStudy: A kiosk logs three orders: 2 notebooks at 500 each, 1 pen at 200, and 3 folders at 300. The owner wants total sales and a calculation that will remain correct when tomorrow’s data is added.
steps: Enter Quantity and UnitPrice as numeric fields
Calculate LineSales = Quantity × UnitPrice
Convert the data to a structured table and sum LineSales
Add one order and verify the total updates
modules.workedExample: Line sales = 2×500 = 1,000; 1×200 = 200; 3×300 = 900. Total = 2,100. In an Excel Table, use =SUM(Orders[LineSales]).
modules.interpretation: A total is a sum of line values, not a sum of quantities or an average of unit prices. Document whether refunds and discounts are included.
modules.microProject: Add a fourth order of 2 pens at 200 and calculate the revised total; list the Excel formula.
modules.modelAnswer: New line sales = 400; revised total = 2,500. In a worksheet: =SUM(D2:D5), where D contains the calculated line totals.
modules.commonMistake: Do not sum textual ID columns or assume formatting a cell changes its underlying data type.
modules.next: Continue with the Excel Analytics weeks 1–4.

modules.title: First SQL queries
modules.outcome: Read a table and return only the records needed for a business question.
modules.prerequisites: F01; understand what a row and column represent.
modules.lesson: SQL describes the result you want from a relational database. SELECT chooses fields, FROM selects a source, WHERE checks which individual rows qualify, and ORDER BY determines the output order. A primary key identifies one row; a foreign key connects related tables. Unlike a spreadsheet, a database does not promise an inherent row order. Use AND/OR parentheses and NULL-aware predicates, because missing values are not identical to zero or an empty string.
modules.caseStudy: A merchant asks for completed East-region orders, highest value first. The orders table contains order_id, region, status and amount. A read-only query answers the request without changing records.
steps: Inspect the table columns and identify the order grain
Write SELECT with necessary fields only
Add status and region filters
Sort descending with a stable tie-break and inspect totals
modules.workedExample: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed' AND region = 'East' ORDER BY amount DESC, order_id;
modules.interpretation: The output contains individual East orders only; it is not a regional total. To obtain a sum, learn aggregation rather than adding a misleading label.
modules.microProject: Change the filter to return West completed orders worth at least 5,000, largest first.
modules.modelAnswer: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed' AND region = 'West' AND amount >= 5000 ORDER BY amount DESC, order_id;
modules.commonMistake: LIMIT without ORDER BY can return an unpredictable sample; = NULL will not test missing values.
modules.next: Continue with SQL weeks 1–3 and try the SQL Practice Arena.

modules.title: Python from zero
modules.outcome: Write short, readable Python scripts that calculate and label a business result.
modules.prerequisites: F01; no prior coding experience.
modules.lesson: Python lets you express an analysis as reproducible instructions. A variable stores a value, a list stores an ordered collection, and a dictionary pairs field names with values. A loop repeats a calculation, while a function packages a reusable step. An if statement controls branches based on a Boolean condition. Use descriptive names and small functions; a script that appears to run is not necessarily correct until you inspect its inputs and expected output.
modules.caseStudy: A small shop has order values [1200, 800, 500]. You want a total and an average you can recalculate when new orders arrive. This is a first step toward automated reporting.
steps: Create a list of numeric order amounts
Use sum() and len() with explicit variable names
Handle the empty-list case to avoid division by zero
Print a labelled result and test another list
modules.workedExample:
values = [1200, 800, 500]
total = sum(values)
average = total / len(values) if values else 0
print(total, average)  # 2500 833.333...
modules.interpretation: Total is 2,500 and the mean is about 833.33 per order. It is not a forecast or a per-customer metric.
modules.microProject: Add a fourth order of 1,500. State the new total and average and write the revised code.
modules.modelAnswer: 4,000 total and 1,000 average: values.append(1500); total=sum(values); average=total/len(values).
modules.commonMistake: Never divide by len(values) without handling empty input; never confuse quoted numbers with numeric values.
modules.next: Continue with Python fundamentals and the Python Practice Arena.

modules.title: Statistics you can explain
modules.outcome: Describe a small dataset while communicating spread, sample size and uncertainty.
modules.prerequisites: F02; basic arithmetic.
modules.lesson: Descriptive statistics reduce many observations to useful summaries. The mean is sensitive to extreme values; the median is often more representative of a skewed distribution. Spread matters because two groups can have the same average but very different consistency. Also identify whether the numbers cover every customer or only a sample. A sample estimate is not a guaranteed description of a population, especially when the collection process excludes some groups.
modules.caseStudy: Five delivery times in minutes are 10, 11, 12, 12 and 35. The manager asks for a “typical delivery time” and whether there is a delay problem.
steps: Order the values and compute mean and median
Identify the long-tail observation
Write what the mean and median each communicate
Propose one additional measurement before acting
modules.workedExample: Mean = (10+11+12+12+35)/5 = 16 minutes. Median = 12 minutes. Range = 35−10 = 25 minutes.
modules.interpretation: Most jobs are near 12 minutes but one took 35 minutes. Investigate the outlier rather than automatically deleting it.
modules.microProject: A second courier has times 12,12,12,12,12. Both groups have median 12; explain how service reliability differs.
modules.modelAnswer: The second courier has zero observed range while the first ranges over 25 minutes; similar median does not mean similar predictability.
modules.commonMistake: Averages alone hide outliers and sampling bias. A small sample cannot establish a stable service-level agreement.
modules.next: Continue with Statistics weeks 1–5.

modules.title: Clean data and protect people
modules.outcome: Identify data quality problems without losing traceability or exposing private information.
modules.prerequisites: F01–F02; basic tables.
modules.lesson: Quality is not simply deleting blanks. Completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency and timeliness each require a business rule. A missing delivery date may be correct for an open order but invalid for a completed order. Preserve the raw input and log transformations; record how many rows were changed or excluded. Treat names, phone numbers and account IDs as sensitive when they identify a person. Use small synthetic datasets in exercises and share only what a learning task actually needs.
modules.caseStudy: A CSV has 100 orders, five repeated IDs and six missing completion dates. Four of the missing dates belong to still-open orders. A safe quality report distinguishes expected blanks from data errors.
steps: Define rules based on order status
Count duplicate keys and affected records
Separate acceptable from invalid missing dates
Create a reconciliation log and redact personally identifying fields
modules.workedExample: Of six missing completion dates, only two are exceptions if the other four belong to open orders. Report “2 invalid completed orders” rather than “6 corrupt rows.”
modules.interpretation: Dedupe rules require evidence: repeated IDs may represent accidental duplication or legitimate source updates. Do not delete before inspecting their business meaning.
modules.microProject: List three checks for a customer sales table and say which columns you would mask in a public learning example.
modules.modelAnswer: Checks: unique order ID, nonnegative sale amount, required completion date for completed status. Mask customer name, phone number and email.
modules.commonMistake: Replacing unknown amounts with zero biases financial totals; never publish personal records to a classroom sandbox.
modules.next: Continue with Power Query weeks 2–3 and Data Analysis week 8.

modules.title: Visuals that support decisions
modules.outcome: Choose appropriate charts and write one correct, evidence-based insight.
modules.prerequisites: F01–F05; an understanding of percentages.
modules.lesson: Visual design begins with the question. Compare categories with bars and change over time with lines; use a scatterplot only when investigating the relationship between two quantitative variables. Label units, periods and population. Avoid truncated bar-chart axes that exaggerate differences, and never put incompatible scales on one axis. An insight should state the observed pattern, its likely operational relevance, and what remains unknown.
modules.caseStudy: A weekly sales dashboard shows East = 120,000 and West = 80,000 over the same seven days. A regional manager wants to allocate follow-up calls.
steps: Define the aggregation and time filter
Choose a horizontal bar chart with zero baseline
Annotate the values and relevant comparison
Write an observation plus one question for further analysis
modules.workedExample: East contributes 120,000 / 200,000 = 60% of the observed two-region revenue; West contributes 40%.
modules.interpretation: Being 60% of revenue does not mean East is 60% more profitable. Profit requires expenses, returns and margins.
modules.microProject: Pick a chart for monthly sales trend and one for order value by category; say why each fits.
modules.modelAnswer: Line chart for month-to-month trend; bar chart for category comparisons. Both need clear labels, an explicit period and a consistent metric.
modules.commonMistake: Do not infer causality from chart shape or compare values from different populations without normalization.
modules.next: Continue with Power BI or Tableau weeks 1–3.

modules.title: Excel formulas and self-updating dashboards
modules.outcome: Build reusable, auditable spreadsheet models with dynamic formulas and summary views.
modules.prerequisites: F02, F05; comfortable with formulas and basic tables.
modules.lesson: As workbooks grow, avoid copying the same hard-coded formula into many cells. Structured references name the business fields, XLOOKUP connects a fact table to a dimension, SUMIFS aggregates with explicit conditions, and LET assigns readable names to parts of a calculation. Dynamic arrays spill variable-sized results into adjacent cells; keep the spill area free. Validate each formula against a manually checked small dataset, and put the data grain and refresh date on the dashboard.
modules.caseStudy: A shop receives new rows daily. The owner needs completed revenue by region, with a product lookup for cost and a gross-margin KPI that updates after new orders.
steps: Create named Excel Tables for Orders and Products
Use XLOOKUP to populate unit cost and LET to name intermediate metrics
Build a PivotTable or SUMIFS summary with month and region filters
Compare dashboard totals against the raw table and document omissions
modules.workedExample: =LET(sales, SUMIFS(Orders[Revenue],Orders[Status],"Completed"), cost, SUMIFS(Orders[Cost],Orders[Status],"Completed"), IFERROR((sales-cost)/sales,0))
modules.interpretation: Gross margin is (revenue−cost)/revenue, not profit divided by cost. A zero-revenue case needs deliberate handling rather than a hidden error.
modules.microProject: Given completed sales of 200,000 and cost of 150,000, calculate gross margin and explain the denominator.
modules.modelAnswer: 25%: (200,000−150,000)/200,000. Revenue is the denominator because margin is the share of sales retained after costs.
modules.commonMistake: Gross margin differs from net margin; spill formulas do not work identically in every older Excel version.
modules.next: Take Excel weeks 4–10, then progress to dbt and warehouse modelling.

modules.title: Relational SQL: joins, CTEs and windows
modules.outcome: Write trustworthy multi-table analyses while preventing duplicated revenue and misplaced filters.
modules.prerequisites: F03; SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.
modules.lesson: A join combines tables based on related keys, but it can also multiply rows: an order with three lines appears three times after joining headers to lines. Know the grain of each table before aggregating. A CTE makes multi-step logic readable; a window function calculates rankings or running totals without collapsing individual rows. Validate against a known source total and count distinct business keys after any join.
modules.caseStudy: A retailer keeps Orders(order_id, region) and Lines(order_id, product_id, amount). Operations wants revenue by region and the top-selling product without counting each header repeatedly.
steps: Check uniqueness on the order and line keys
Join lines to orders and sum line amount by region
Use a CTE to aggregate product revenue
Use DENSE_RANK over revenue to identify top products and reconcile totals
modules.workedExample: WITH product_sales AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM lines GROUP BY product_id) SELECT product_id,revenue,DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rank_no FROM product_sales;
modules.interpretation: The ranking is across products because the window has no PARTITION BY. Add PARTITION BY region only after a region column exists in the grouped result.
modules.microProject: A header has total 100 and three line records of 20,30,50. Why does SUM(header.total) after a join return 300, and what would you sum instead?
modules.modelAnswer: The header value repeats on every line (3×100). Sum line amount = 100, or pre-aggregate at order grain before joining.
modules.commonMistake: SELECT DISTINCT is not a reliable fix for a bad join; it may hide duplicate records instead of reconciling the grain.
modules.next: Take SQL weeks 4–10 and write reconciliation tests.

modules.title: Power Query and repeatable ETL
modules.outcome: Create a refreshable extract-transform-load flow with explicit cleaning and quality checks.
modules.prerequisites: F02, F06; basic spreadsheet transformations.
modules.lesson: Power Query records a reproducible set of transformation steps. First inspect source fields and types, then apply changes deliberately: parse dates with the right locale, remove or flag invalid values, append similar files and merge dimension fields using verified join keys. Unpivot repeated month columns into tidy rows before analysis. A good pipeline is idempotent: rerunning it with the same input produces the same output. Record input row counts and exceptions so refresh failures are visible.
modules.caseStudy: A training company collects Jan and Feb attendance files, but one file writes dates as DD/MM/YYYY and the other as ISO dates. The owner wants one monthly participation report.
steps: Append the files without deleting source copies
Apply date parsing per source and normalize status codes
Merge the course lookup on a unique course ID
Group monthly counts and log invalid rows
modules.workedExample: M example: Table.TransformColumnTypes(Source, {{"Date", type date}, {"Attended", Int64.Type}}, "en-GB")
modules.interpretation: The locale affects how dates are parsed, not merely how they display. A mistaken locale can silently move attendance between months.
modules.microProject: Describe why January and February data should be appended rather than merged when the columns represent the same fields.
modules.modelAnswer: Append stacks rows for the same schema; merge adds columns using key matches. Check the combined row count equals the input counts, less documented exclusions.
modules.commonMistake: Removing errors silently makes totals unreliable; inspect the cause and report exclusions.
modules.next: Take the Power Query course and learn orchestration at A-level.

modules.title: Python pandas and exploratory analysis
modules.outcome: Profile, clean and summarize a dataset with reproducible code and interpretable outputs.
modules.prerequisites: F04–F06; functions, lists and descriptive statistics.
modules.lesson: A pandas DataFrame is an in-memory table with labelled columns. Loading a CSV is not the same as validating it: check dtypes, null counts, duplicates and business keys before computing a result. GroupBy summarizes by categories, while merge can accidentally duplicate records when a lookup key is not unique. A notebook should explain why each transformation is appropriate, not only display the output. For reproducibility, freeze the sample dataset, seed any randomized steps and keep assertions on known totals.
modules.caseStudy: You receive 200 synthetic orders with region, status, amount and refund. The business wants net revenue by region and a list of suspicious duplicates.
steps: Read the file and inspect shape, dtypes and nulls
Flag duplicate order IDs and resolve them with a documented rule
Define net revenue and filter completed orders
Group by region, check source totals, and plot a labelled comparison
modules.workedExample: net = df.loc[df['status'].eq('Completed')].assign(net=lambda x:x.amount-x.refund); net.groupby('region')['net'].sum()
modules.interpretation: `net` must be defined at a consistent row grain; subtracting refunds from unrelated rows would overstate or understate revenue.
modules.microProject: Explain why `df.drop_duplicates()` without a business key can be dangerous on an order dataset.
modules.modelAnswer: Identical-looking rows may reflect real repeated purchases, while two versions of one ID may differ. Verify an order key and update policy before deduplicating.
modules.commonMistake: EDA patterns are observations, not causal findings; redact or synthesize personal data in shared notebooks.
modules.next: Continue to statistical inference, forecasting and production ML.

modules.title: Power BI modelling and DAX
modules.outcome: Build correct measures that respond predictably to filters and support business decisions.
modules.prerequisites: F02, F05, F07 and basic SQL joins.
modules.lesson: A Power BI report depends on its semantic model. Store transactions in fact tables and descriptive attributes in dimension tables with clear one-to-many relationships. Measures calculate at query time in the filter context created by slicers and visuals; calculated columns materialize during refresh. CALCULATE changes filter context, so denominator choice requires care. A robust report reconciles grand totals and makes users aware of the time window and units.
modules.caseStudy: A workforce report measures assigned hours against available hours by team. Management asks whether 80% team utilization means each person is near 80%.
steps: Model Resources, Dates and Allocations with documented keys
Write total assigned and available hours measures
Calculate weighted utilization with DIVIDE
Test a single resource, then team and date slicers and compare totals
modules.workedExample: Utilization % = DIVIDE(SUM(Allocations[AssignedHours]), SUM(Capacity[AvailableHours]))
modules.interpretation: The team ratio is weighted by available hours, not necessarily the unweighted average of individual utilization percentages.
modules.microProject: Two people have 20/40 and 36/40 assigned hours. Calculate weighted team utilization.
modules.modelAnswer: (20+36)/(40+40) = 70%. The arithmetic average of 50% and 90% also happens to be 70% here because capacity is equal.
modules.commonMistake: Be careful with many-to-many relationships and denominators altered by filters; validate each context.
modules.next: Take Power BI weeks 3–10 and progress to enterprise modelling.

modules.title: Tableau and evidence-led storytelling
modules.outcome: Build an interactive, accessible view that guides users from an observation to a next action.
topics: Calculated fields, LOD and table calculations
modules.prerequisites: F05, F07; comfort with categorical and time-series data.
modules.lesson: Tableau creates views by combining dimensions, measures and visual encodings. First decide the unit of analysis, then place a metric in the view and test the aggregation. Tableau LOD calculations fix or change the aggregation scope independently of some view details; table calculations operate over the marks in the rendered partition. Interactive filters should clarify the result rather than make it impossible to compare periods. Provide explicit units, colour-safe labels and tooltips with key definitions.
modules.caseStudy: A retail operations analyst wants to identify which branch is falling behind the prior quarter. A dashboard should let a manager filter region, inspect the branch, and read the relevant contribution to the decline.
steps: Create a trend with correctly ordered dates
Build a region comparison and a metric definition tooltip
Add a parameter or action to inspect one branch
Add a short caveat and check dashboard behaviour at mobile width
modules.workedExample: Example calculated field: SUM([Sales]) / SUM([Orders]) — only valid as average order value if [Orders] is a suitable count field at the intended grain.
modules.interpretation: Dividing two aggregated measures is often preferable to averaging per-row ratios. Confirm what an order count represents.
modules.microProject: Create a title and insight sentence for a dashboard where Branch A declines from 100k to 85k.
modules.modelAnswer: “Branch A net sales fell 15% quarter over quarter (100k → 85k); inspect traffic and returns before attributing the change.”
modules.commonMistake: Using an LOD expression does not automatically fix erroneous joins or mismatched grain.
modules.next: Take Tableau weeks 4–10 and compare with Power BI modelling.

modules.title: Inference and experiment literacy
modules.outcome: Interpret confidence intervals, p-values and experiment designs without overstating conclusions.
modules.prerequisites: F05; percentages and basic probability.
modules.lesson: Statistical inference uses sample data to estimate a population quantity under stated assumptions. A confidence interval expresses uncertainty using a procedure that would cover the true fixed value at its advertised rate over repeated samples. A p-value describes how surprising a statistic would be if a null model were true; it is not the probability that the null is true. Before trusting an A/B experiment, verify random assignment, sample size, eligibility and a pre-selected primary metric.
modules.caseStudy: A website tests a shorter checkout. Version A converts 20 of 100 visitors and B converts 24 of 100. The team wants to declare a winner immediately.
steps: Define eligible visitors and conversion before calculating
Compute the observed conversion rates
State the absolute difference and what uncertainty remains
Discuss sample size, randomization and what a significance test would assess
modules.workedExample: A = 20%, B = 24%; observed lift = +4 percentage points (relative lift +20%). This alone is not proof of a repeatable improvement.
modules.interpretation: An apparent 20% relative lift sounds substantial, but only four additional conversions occurred in these small samples.
modules.microProject: Explain the difference between +4 percentage points and +20% relative lift in this example.
modules.modelAnswer: Absolute difference = 24%−20% = 4 points; relative lift = (24−20)/20 = 20% measured against A.
modules.commonMistake: Never stop an experiment early just because the current p-value looks favourable without a valid sequential design.
modules.next: Continue to advanced A/B testing and causal inference.

modules.title: Git and reproducible analysis
modules.outcome: Maintain versioned, reviewable work with tests and a lightweight change log.
topics: Git add, commit, branch and merge
modules.prerequisites: F03 or F04; a small working SQL or Python script.
modules.lesson: Version control tells you what changed, why, and when, making analysis auditable. A repository should keep code, sample synthetic inputs, instructions and tests while excluding secrets and raw personal data. Use descriptive commits, feature branches for experimentation and peer review before merging. Record tool versions and assumptions so another analyst can reproduce the results. A correct analysis with no provenance is hard to maintain or defend.
modules.caseStudy: Two analysts share a weekly revenue query. One quietly changes how refunds are handled; the reported number changes without an explanation.
steps: Create a repository with a README and synthetic sample
Commit the initial query and expected total
Create a branch for refund handling and add a test
Review the diff, explain the changed metric and merge
modules.workedExample: Example commit flow: git switch -c fix/refunds; git add revenue.sql tests/; git commit -m "Account for completed-order refunds"
modules.interpretation: The test should record an expected result and fail if a future edit changes it accidentally.
modules.microProject: Write a one-line commit message for fixing a duplicate join and list two files that should never be committed.
modules.modelAnswer: Commit: “Fix order-line fanout in revenue calculation”. Exclude .env with API secrets and raw customer exports.
modules.commonMistake: Git does not replace secure backups or data-access permissions; never place credentials in a training repository.
modules.next: Continue to dbt projects and CI/CD.

modules.title: Production SQL and query performance
modules.outcome: Tune and verify analytic queries without sacrificing correctness.
modules.prerequisites: I02, I08; fluency with joins and window functions.
modules.lesson: Production SQL must be both correct and efficient. The optimizer selects a plan using table statistics, estimated cardinality and available access paths. Examine actual plans and measure the bottleneck before creating indexes or rewriting queries. Filter early when possible, keep predicates searchable, and distinguish OLTP index design from warehouse partition pruning. A slowly changing dimension preserves history so a transaction can be reported using the category valid at the time. Every optimization must preserve row counts and business totals.
modules.caseStudy: A daily sales dashboard is slowing as the orders table reaches millions of rows. A developer suggests adding DISTINCT to every join, masking duplicated revenue rather than fixing the data model.
steps: Capture baseline timing and reconciled totals
Inspect the explain plan for large scans or many-to-many joins
Rewrite the join at a documented grain and test date pruning
Compare execution time, rows and totals after changes
modules.workedExample: SELECT region, SUM(net_amount) FROM fact_orders WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY region;  -- Verify pruning/partition choice in the actual target engine.
modules.interpretation: Query syntax and date types differ by engine. Correctness must be checked independently of performance.
modules.microProject: An order header of 400 joins to four lines. Why is SUM(header_amount) = 1,600 and what source should control the total?
modules.modelAnswer: The header repeats four times. Aggregate transaction line amounts or a one-row-per-order intermediate table, then reconcile the result to 400.
modules.commonMistake: An index that speeds a demo may slow writes or be ignored by a columnar cloud warehouse.
modules.next: Continue to A02 and A08 for governed transformations.

modules.title: Analytics engineering with dbt and Snowflake
modules.outcome: Build a tested, documented warehouse transformation project that preserves metric meaning.
modules.prerequisites: I02 and I08; query validation and Git basics.
modules.lesson: Modern analytics engineering treats transformations like software. Stage source fields without altering business logic, use intermediate models for reusable joins and build marts at clearly defined grains. In dbt, `ref()` expresses dependencies between models; source declarations document upstream tables. Test uniqueness, relationships and accepted values to detect silent data errors before a dashboard reads them. Decide when a view, table or incremental materialization is appropriate; incremental updates require a sound unique key and late-arriving record strategy.
modules.caseStudy: A subscription service calculates monthly recurring revenue in three dashboards, each with slightly different refund rules. An analytics engineer creates one reviewed revenue mart and publishes its definition.
steps: Define raw sources and a staging contract
Build customer and transaction staging models
Create a monthly revenue mart with an explicit grain
Add tests, documentation and a reconciliation query before deploying
modules.workedExample: dbt source example: SELECT customer_id, SUM(net_amount) AS net_revenue FROM {{ ref('stg_payments') }} GROUP BY customer_id;  -- model tests must enforce customer_id uniqueness in the output.
modules.interpretation: Whether the model is at customer or customer-month grain is part of the contract; date must be included if the latter is intended.
modules.microProject: Choose two data tests for a customer revenue mart and say what each catches.
modules.modelAnswer: Unique customer_id detects unexpected duplicate rows; not_null customer_id prevents unassignable revenue. Add relationship checks where dimensions are required.
modules.commonMistake: Modelling tools cannot compensate for an undefined KPI or incorrect source grain.
modules.next: Explore certified metrics, lineage and CI alongside governance.

modules.title: Orchestrate resilient data pipelines
modules.outcome: Design a scheduled pipeline with retries, dependencies and observable data-quality checks.
modules.prerequisites: I03, I08; reproducible transformations.
modules.lesson: A data pipeline is a directed flow of tasks, not a collection of unrelated scripts. An orchestrator coordinates ingestion, transformation, quality checks and publishing while recording what ran and when. Design each task to be safe to retry: processing the same date twice should not double sales. Watermarks track how far data has arrived; backfills recompute a bounded period after late data. Use failure alerts based on business impact, not just whether a job exited with code zero.
modules.caseStudy: A retailer receives a daily order file at 02:00. A dashboard refresh at 02:05 sometimes reports incomplete revenue because delivery is late.
steps: Define a freshness threshold and arrival check
Ingest only once per batch ID and record row counts
Run transformations and validation after ingestion succeeds
Publish after validation and alert if freshness or totals fail
modules.workedExample: DAG: wait_for_file → ingest_raw → validate_schema → transform_daily → reconcile_totals → publish_report.
modules.interpretation: If validation fails, the publishing task should not run; the previous confirmed dataset should remain available with a freshness warning.
modules.microProject: What happens when the 01 Nov file arrives late after the 02 Nov run, and how would you repair the date window?
modules.modelAnswer: Use a bounded backfill for affected partitions, rerun idempotent tasks and reconcile final totals before republishing. Do not insert duplicate batches.
modules.commonMistake: Blind retries can multiply records or overload source systems if tasks are not idempotent.
modules.next: Move to A04 for cloud architectural decisions.

modules.title: Cloud and lakehouse architecture
modules.outcome: Choose storage, processing and access patterns that fit cost, scale, governance and workload.
modules.prerequisites: I02, I03, I08; SQL and ETL fundamentals.
modules.lesson: Cloud architecture is a sequence of trade-offs rather than one magic service. Object storage handles large durable files; a warehouse offers managed SQL analytics; a lakehouse combines file-based storage with table reliability and computational engines. Separate raw, curated and serving layers and document who can read each. Use least-privilege roles, retention policies and encryption. Choose services according to volume, freshness, concurrency and budget; a small batch workload may not justify an expensive streaming cluster.
modules.caseStudy: A regional health NGO wants monthly aggregate reports from three offices. Data includes personally identifying records and must be accessible only to an approved team.
steps: Classify raw and aggregate fields and residency rules
Sketch landing, curated and reporting layers
Assign restricted IAM roles and retention policies
Estimate workload costs and pick an appropriately simple engine
modules.workedExample: Architecture: restricted bucket → ingestion job → curated table with pseudonymized IDs → SQL reporting view with aggregated counts.
modules.interpretation: Distributing dashboards does not require publishing the raw person-level data. Access controls must be enforced at the storage and query layers.
modules.microProject: Name one reason to choose a warehouse over a Spark cluster for a small daily reporting workload.
modules.modelAnswer: A managed warehouse can run familiar SQL with fewer operational components and often lower total maintenance burden for small, structured batch queries.
modules.commonMistake: Never place secret keys in front-end code or treat region selection as a purely technical preference.
modules.next: Continue to L4 governance, Spark and streaming.

modules.title: Supervised machine learning that generalizes
modules.outcome: Build and evaluate a baseline model with leakage prevention and an honest test set.
modules.prerequisites: I04 and I07; pandas and probability.
modules.lesson: Machine learning learns statistical patterns from examples; it does not inherently uncover causal rules. Define the prediction target and decision deadline first, so you do not include future information as a feature. Split data according to the use case: time-based data often needs temporal validation rather than random splitting. Begin with a simple baseline, choose metrics aligned with error costs, and inspect performance across groups. Document model limitations and never claim a strong accuracy score without saying what dataset produced it.
modules.caseStudy: A shop predicts next-week stockouts from prior sales and supply lead time. Using the actual future stockout quantity as a feature produces an unrealistic near-perfect model.
steps: Define the point of prediction and available features
Build a time-based holdout set
Train a simple classifier against a no-skill baseline
Compare precision/recall on a held-out period and check leakage
modules.workedExample: If 8 out of 10 predicted stockouts are genuine, precision = 80%. If there were 20 actual stockouts and the model found 8, recall = 40%.
modules.interpretation: An 80% precision model may still miss most stockouts. Choose a threshold based on the cost of missed shortages versus false alarms.
modules.microProject: Which metric is more useful if missing a stockout is very costly: precision or recall, and why?
modules.modelAnswer: Recall is usually prioritized because it measures how many actual stockouts were found; still monitor precision so false alarms remain manageable.
modules.commonMistake: Do not normalize or impute using all rows before splitting; it leaks test information into training.
modules.next: Continue to L4 MLOps, drift and responsible deployment.

modules.title: A/B testing and causal evidence
modules.outcome: Design, analyze and communicate an experiment with a valid primary metric.
modules.prerequisites: I07; sample inference, proportions and business metrics.
modules.lesson: Controlled experiments attempt to estimate a treatment effect by comparing randomized groups. Define the hypothesis, allocation unit, primary metric and stopping rule before launch. Check whether users remain in assigned groups and whether sample ratios match the plan. A result can be statistically detectable but economically unimportant, or useful but too uncertain to make a decision. Watch guardrails such as refunds and latency so optimizing one metric does not cause collateral damage.
modules.caseStudy: A checkout layout test appears to increase conversion, but the treatment group receives fewer mobile users due to a tracking bug.
steps: Pre-register the conversion outcome and mobile guardrails
Audit randomization and sample-ratio balance
Calculate effect size and an appropriate uncertainty interval
Decide whether to ship, extend or invalidate the experiment and document the rationale
modules.workedExample: A converts 200/1,000 = 20%; B converts 220/1,000 = 22%. Observed uplift = +2 percentage points, or +10% relative.
modules.interpretation: The difference is an estimate. Statistical confidence requires an uncertainty calculation and a valid randomization and measurement process.
modules.microProject: Treatment causes refunds to rise from 1% to 4%. Should a conversion lift alone justify rollout?
modules.modelAnswer: No. Evaluate the refund guardrail and business value; a higher conversion rate may be offset by costly negative effects.
modules.commonMistake: A significant p-value does not repair broken assignment, multiple unplanned analyses or a biased measurement pipeline.
modules.next: Continue to causal methods and monitoring.

modules.title: Time series and forecasting
modules.outcome: Build a defensible forecast with seasonal baselines and error analysis.
modules.prerequisites: I04 and I07; date handling and descriptive statistics.
modules.lesson: Forecasting is about predicting future observations using information available at the forecast origin. Begin with a naive or seasonal-naive baseline; complex models are only useful when they outperform this. Keep the training and evaluation periods ordered in time to prevent future leakage. Measure accuracy using an appropriate metric: percentage error is unstable around zero, while mean absolute error remains interpretable in original units. Explain uncertainty and the operational cost of over- or under-forecasting.
modules.caseStudy: A warehouse forecasts weekly demand for a product that sells more during holidays. A random train/test split mixes future holiday patterns into the past and overstates accuracy.
steps: Visualize demand by week and annotate major events
Define the horizon and seasonal baseline
Backtest on successive future windows
Compare MAE and bias; describe limitations and uncertainty
modules.workedExample: Actual demand [100,120] and forecasts [90,130] yield absolute errors [10,10] and MAE = 10 units.
modules.interpretation: A MAE of 10 is only useful compared with stockout and inventory costs and a baseline such as last-week demand.
modules.microProject: If a model systematically underforecasts holiday weeks by 20 units, what operational risk follows?
modules.modelAnswer: Understocking and missed sales; add an event/holiday indicator or increase safety stock while validating on past holiday windows.
modules.commonMistake: Do not evaluate time-series models on randomly shuffled data or declare precision without uncertainty.
modules.next: Continue to ML deployment and alerting.

modules.title: Data contracts, quality tests and CI/CD
modules.outcome: Enforce reliable schemas, freshness and business reconciliations before publishing downstream data.
modules.prerequisites: I03, I08 and A02; SQL transformations and Git workflow.
modules.lesson: Production pipelines fail in ways that look like success: a source adds a new status code, a late partition arrives, or a join quietly doubles transactions. A data contract defines expected types, allowed keys and freshness standards between teams. Test each layer’s correctness and reconcile significant business totals before releases. CI runs checks on every change; deployment promotion should be possible to reverse, with incident owners and clear rollback procedures.
modules.caseStudy: An upstream team changes amount from numeric to formatted text. Reports still refresh but net revenue becomes null for part of the month.
steps: Define amount type and non-null rules in a source contract
Add a duplicate-key and daily total check
Run tests in CI against representative fixtures
Quarantine invalid batches and publish a failure status instead of a misleading total
modules.workedExample: Example test: number of completed orders in curated data = source completed order count ± documented exclusions.
modules.interpretation: A quality test should express a business invariant, not only the absence of SQL exceptions.
modules.microProject: Give one semantic test a report should pass before being released, beyond checking a column data type.
modules.modelAnswer: Revenue reconciles within a documented tolerance to the source ledger for the same dates, status rules and currency; explain deviations.
modules.commonMistake: Passing unit tests does not guarantee correctness if they only assert that code runs rather than what numbers mean.
modules.next: Continue to real-time observability and governance.

modules.title: Distributed computing with Spark
modules.outcome: Explain partitioned execution and choose Spark operations that avoid unnecessary shuffles.
modules.prerequisites: A01, A03, A04; SQL, partitioning and pipelines.
modules.lesson: Spark distributes data processing across worker executors. Operations such as filtering and simple projections are often local to partitions; joins and groupings may trigger a network shuffle. Big data performance depends on data size, partition layout and key distribution—not only writing short code. DataFrame transformations are lazy until an action runs. Open table formats can add transaction semantics and schema evolution to object storage, but each format has its own feature support and operational trade-offs.
modules.caseStudy: A telecom data lake receives millions of call records daily. Grouping by country works, but one extremely common country key slows a shuffle stage and causes skew.
steps: Describe the record grain and daily partition strategy
Inspect stage metrics and locate the skewed grouping key
Filter early and consider targeted salting or re-partitioning only after measurement
Validate total record counts and billable amounts after tuning
modules.workedExample: Pseudocode: df.filter("date >= date_sub(current_date(), 7)").groupBy("region").count() — partition pruning requires matching the physical layout.
modules.interpretation: Running groupBy can produce a shuffle. Verify skew using task metrics; repartitioning blindly may increase costs.
modules.microProject: Why does one very frequent join key cause slow tasks even when many executors are available?
modules.modelAnswer: Rows with the same key may concentrate in a few partitions, creating long-running straggler tasks and unbalanced work.
modules.commonMistake: Caching every DataFrame can exhaust memory; do not assume a cloud cluster removes data-quality responsibilities.
modules.next: Continue to E07 for scalable lakehouse lifecycle design.

modules.title: Streaming analytics with Kafka
modules.outcome: Design a near-real-time event flow with defined delivery guarantees and late-event handling.
modules.prerequisites: A03, A04 and E01; batch ETL and distributed concepts.
modules.lesson: Streaming systems read an unbounded flow of events and update results as new information arrives. Kafka topics are partitioned append-only logs; consumer groups coordinate readers and manage offsets. Differentiate event time (when something happened) from processing time (when the system saw it). Watermarks limit how long late events can revise an aggregate. Delivery guarantees depend on the entire pipeline, including external sinks; claiming “exactly once” without end-to-end evidence is unsafe.
modules.caseStudy: A payments platform flags a surge of failed transactions over five-minute event-time windows. Network delays cause some failures to arrive after their original interval.
steps: Define an event key and event-time field
Choose topic partitions and a consumer group
Aggregate per event-time window with a documented watermark
Write idempotently to the sink and monitor lag and missing partitions
modules.workedExample: If failures per five-minute window increase from 10 to 35, the observed increment is 25; alert thresholds should also account for volume and known outages.
modules.interpretation: A late event may update an earlier window if it arrives within the allowed lateness; outside it, the system needs a documented policy.
modules.microProject: Explain why counting consumed messages without deduplicating by stable transaction ID can overstate payments.
modules.modelAnswer: At-least-once delivery may replay an event after retries. Use an idempotent sink or dedupe by event ID and explain any retention window.
modules.commonMistake: Kafka does not automatically guarantee one row per business event in every downstream database.
modules.next: Continue to E08 incident exercises and observability.

modules.title: MLOps: deployment and monitoring
modules.outcome: Operate a model with reproducible versions, drift checks, monitoring and rollback.
modules.prerequisites: A05, A08; model evaluation and pipeline quality.
modules.lesson: An accurate notebook is not a production model. Production requires pinned dependencies, artifact and data versioning, tested feature transformations, and monitored serving. Separate prediction latency, error rate, feature distributions and real-world target quality because drift may occur long before labels become available. Define rollback criteria and an owner for investigations. Monitor error slices for affected groups; aggregate accuracy can hide systematic failures for a smaller population.
modules.caseStudy: A churn predictor trained on last year’s users degrades when the subscription product changes. Weekly serving continues without an error, but accuracy drops in a new user segment.
steps: Register model version and training data signature
Deploy with monitored feature schema and latency
Compare incoming features with training distribution and evaluate labelled outcomes
Trigger investigation, fallback or rollback when guardrails fail
modules.workedExample: A model with overall 90% accuracy but 55% accuracy on a new segment requires slice-level review even if its global KPI looks healthy.
modules.interpretation: Operational monitoring is broader than model accuracy: track drift, outages, missing features, outcomes and business costs.
modules.microProject: Name two signals to monitor before delayed ground-truth labels are available.
modules.modelAnswer: Input schema/feature drift and serving latency or error rate; label-based precision/recall cannot be trusted until labels arrive.
modules.commonMistake: Retraining automatically on unvalidated drift can reinforce bias or learn from corrupted data.
modules.next: Continue to E04 and responsible AI controls.

modules.title: Deep learning, embeddings and RAG
modules.outcome: Explain neural models and build a source-grounded retrieval-augmented question-answering prototype.
modules.prerequisites: A05 and Python fluency; E03 recommended.
modules.lesson: Deep learning uses trainable layered representations to capture complex relationships. Large language models generate tokens conditioned on context and do not verify truth by default. Retrieval-augmented generation first searches a document corpus, then gives relevant passages to the model as supporting context. The system must evaluate retrieval accuracy separately from answer correctness and abstain when documents do not support a claim. Embeddings encode semantic similarity, not legal permission or factual reliability.
modules.caseStudy: A company wants an internal policy assistant. A naive chatbot invents a leave allowance. A retrieval-based assistant must answer from approved, versioned HR policy paragraphs with citations.
steps: Split approved policy text into labelled chunks
Embed and index chunks with restricted access metadata
Retrieve relevant chunks and instruct the model to cite them
Test answer accuracy, missing-answer abstention and document permissions
modules.workedExample: Question: “How many days of leave?” If no retrieved policy passage states a number, a correct response is “The available policy excerpts do not specify the allowance.”
modules.interpretation: Responding with a plausible generic leave figure is a failure because it is not grounded in the organization’s source.
modules.microProject: Explain one reason a semantic search result can be relevant but still unsafe to display.
modules.modelAnswer: The passage may be outdated, restricted to another team or contain confidential data. Enforce document access and effective-date checks.
modules.commonMistake: RAG reduces some hallucinations but cannot eliminate them; prompt text never substitutes for access controls.
modules.next: Continue to E05 prompt evaluation and E06 governance.

modules.title: Prompt engineering, GenAI evaluation and agents
modules.outcome: Use generative AI to support data work while proving correctness and controlling tool access.
topics: Evaluation sets, costs and human review
modules.prerequisites: I04, I08 and E04; SQL/Python basics.
modules.lesson: A productive data prompt provides context, input schema, allowed methods, output format, and checks. Asking a model to “analyze the data” is less reliable than asking for specific SQL with a known definition and an expected reconciliation test. Evaluate the model on representative examples, including adversarial inputs and deliberate missing data. If an agent can call tools, limit its permissions and separate read actions from approvals to publish or mutate records. Generated charts, formulas and narratives still require human validation.
modules.caseStudy: A reporting assistant proposes SQL that multiplies revenue after joining order headers to lines. Its explanation is eloquent, but the number fails reconciliation.
steps: Write a task specification with table grains and metric definition
Request a read-only SQL result and an accompanying validation query
Compare counts and totals with a trusted fixture
Log success, failure, cost and whether a reviewer approved the output
modules.workedExample: Prompt frame: “Use only the listed synthetic tables. Return SQL and a validation query. State the order grain. Do not claim the result is audited unless totals reconcile.”
modules.interpretation: The model response is a draft. Passing a deterministic assertion is stronger evidence than sounding confident.
modules.microProject: An AI query reports revenue 300 from three order lines whose actual total is 100. What test should reject it?
modules.modelAnswer: Assert that grouped line revenue equals the source line sum (100) at the same date/status grain; flag or block the 300 result.
modules.commonMistake: Never upload private records to an unapproved external AI service or let a prompt override enforced role permissions.
modules.next: Continue to E06 security and E08 expert capstone.

modules.title: Data governance, privacy and security
modules.outcome: Create enforceable controls for access, lineage, quality, retention and responsible data sharing.
modules.prerequisites: F06, A04, A08; cloud access and data-quality basics.
modules.lesson: Data governance defines who owns information, what it means and how it may safely be used. A catalog is useful only when important fields have stewards, definitions and lineage to trusted sources. Security begins at storage and service permissions; hiding a button in the browser does not prevent direct API access. Use least privilege, row/column-level controls, encryption and rotation of credentials. Set data retention according to legal and operational requirements and prepare a clear incident response path.
modules.caseStudy: A university analytics app exposes learner scores. A viewer should see only their own progress, while instructors need verified access to cohorts they are assigned to.
steps: Classify user IDs, grades and enrolment information
Define role-to-data access rules at the database layer
Test unauthorized direct API requests and log access
Document retention and data-subject request workflows
modules.workedExample: Access matrix: Learner → own progress; Instructor → assigned cohort aggregated results; Admin → permitted management scope; Public → no private records.
modules.interpretation: The user interface should reflect permissions, but database row-level security and server checks must enforce them.
modules.microProject: Why is hiding the “Admin” menu insufficient to secure learner records?
modules.modelAnswer: An attacker could call the database or API directly. Policies must be enforced server-side and in RLS, with tests for denied access.
modules.commonMistake: Never publish real learner data in demonstrations, tests or reusable prompts.
modules.next: Continue to E08 governance review and incident response.

modules.title: Lakehouse engineering and interoperability
modules.outcome: Design a scalable, maintainable lakehouse with transactional table formats and clear data contracts.
modules.prerequisites: A02, A04, E01; warehouse models and distributed storage.
modules.lesson: Object files alone do not provide a reliable analytical table. Lakehouse formats add metadata and transactional behaviour so readers can obtain consistent snapshots during updates. A layered architecture retains raw provenance, applies validated transformations and exposes purpose-built serving tables. Catalogs help resolve which table is authoritative and who may access it. Choose table format and compute engines with compatibility, upgrade paths, file sizes and retention requirements in mind; avoid promising universal interchangeability.
modules.caseStudy: A business maintains a year of transaction history in object storage. Analysts repeatedly scan tiny CSV files and disagree over whether a failed load created partial totals.
steps: Define raw landing with immutable batch identifiers
Transform to validated partitioned silver transactions
Publish a gold daily-revenue mart with reconciled totals
Plan compaction, schema changes, snapshots and rollback testing
modules.workedExample: Example contract: gold_daily_revenue has one row per business_date and region; its sum for a day must match accepted silver transactions.
modules.interpretation: An ACID table format helps with atomic visibility but cannot validate whether a business KPI is defined correctly.
modules.microProject: What is the purpose of keeping an immutable raw/bronze layer after creating cleaned tables?
modules.modelAnswer: It enables reprocessing, tracing source errors and auditing transformation decisions without needing to reconstruct the original input.
modules.commonMistake: Do not delete historical files solely for short-term performance without checking recovery, compliance and retention needs.
modules.next: Complete E08 with batch, streaming, BI and ML paths.

modules.title: Expert capstone: governed data product
modules.tools: SQL, Git, cloud, BI, Spark, ML
modules.outcome: Explain and prototype an end-to-end data product with quality gates, secure access and monitored outcomes.
topics: Model/LLM checks, incident and cost review
modules.prerequisites: Complete one advanced engineering module, one analytical module and the governance module.
modules.lesson: A strong portfolio capstone shows a business problem, a data contract, reproducible transformations and a measurable decision—not a collection of screenshots. State boundaries: simulated architecture is fine for a mobile learning lab, but do not claim cloud infrastructure was deployed when it was only designed. Provide a traceable chain from raw inputs through reconciled metrics to a dashboard, prediction or alert. Document failure modes, access scopes, rollback criteria and the cost/latency trade-off.
modules.caseStudy: A fictional logistics operator wants daily delivery KPIs, a five-minute delay alert and a stockout predictor. Records arrive from different sources with late updates and limited permissions.
steps: Draw source, raw, curated and serving layers and specify grains
Create SQL/Python pseudocode with three deterministic quality tests
Propose a dashboard, event-time alert and model evaluation plan
Write an access matrix, monitoring SLA and one-page incident runbook
modules.workedExample: Minimum evidence: daily on-time rate = on-time deliveries / eligible completed deliveries; reconcile eligible counts, reject negative transit time, and verify duplicate delivery IDs do not inflate results.
modules.interpretation: The product should explain what it knows, what data is missing and what failures prevent a trusted decision.
modules.microProject: A pipeline reports 95% on-time delivery but 15% of completed orders lack arrival timestamps. Should the dashboard show “verified 95%” without qualification?
modules.modelAnswer: No. Fail or qualify the metric, publish the coverage rate and investigate missing arrivals. A valid service rate needs a defined eligible population.
modules.commonMistake: Do not substitute demo diagrams for a running service or present simulated test results as production evidence.
modules.next: Publish a portfolio README, limitations, versioned assets and an honest validation checklist.
